headline: Sensex adds 1,718 points to 81,028 on Dhanteras, capping its best week in six years as foreign buying pours in
summary: The Sensex climbed 1,718.01 points, or 2.17%, to 81,028.02 on Friday and the Nifty 50 rose 493.75 points, or 2.01%, to 25,030.35, back above 25,000 for a seventh straight gain. Over the week the Sensex rose about 8.8% and the Nifty about 8.6%, their best week since February 2021, though both are still down about 4-5% for 2026. Private banks led the day, while smaller stocks lagged: more shares fell than rose across the market. Reports credited foreign investors, who bought about ₹14,975 crore of Indian shares on Thursday, their largest single-day purchase in nearly six years, along with Brent crude near $100 and India's low exposure to the AI stocks that crashed abroad.
concept_note: When foreign funds rush to buy Indian shares while few holders want to sell, prices have to climb until buyers and sellers balance again. That push and pull that sets a price is what the market equilibrium card explains.
teaser_title: While Tokyo and Seoul crashed 6%, Dalal Street rose 2% and logged its best week in six years.
teaser: Foreign investors pulled money out of AI-heavy markets and parked a record sum in India. Seven straight gains followed. The market equilibrium card shows how a rush of buyers pushes prices up.

headline: AI rout hits Asia: Nikkei and Kospi close about 6% lower, and Seoul halts trading for 20 minutes
summary: Thursday's crash in US AI and chip stocks spread to Asia on Friday. Japan's Nikkei 225 closed about 6% lower at 57,434.77, under 60,000 for the first time in nearly six months, and posted its worst week since 2020. South Korea's Kospi also ended about 6% down after falling more than 8% at one point, which set off a 20-minute trading halt, and Taiwan's Taiex lost about 4.5%. Chipmakers such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix fell steeply in early trade. Reports linked the selling to worries that the Democrats' control of the US Congress could slow data-centre building and bring tighter rules for the AI industry.
concept_note: The chip companies' products and prices did not change overnight; what changed was how much investors wanted to own their shares at any price. A drop in desire at every price is a shift of the whole demand curve, as the change in demand card explains.
teaser_title: Korea paused its stock market for 20 minutes. The trigger was an election across the Pacific.
teaser: Japan and Korea's markets each lost about 6% as the AI selloff crossed the Pacific. The chip companies themselves had not changed. The change in demand card explains why prices fall when buyers lose interest.

headline: US employers add 165,000 jobs in October, far above forecasts; unemployment holds at 4.1%
summary: The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, well above the roughly 55,000-70,000 that economists had expected, according to reports. The unemployment rate stayed at 4.1%, and job gains for August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs and health care 42,000, while average hourly pay rose 0.4% in the month and 3.1% over the year. Reports said the strong numbers raise the odds that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December rather than cut them.
concept_note: Job numbers and interest rates are economic forces that no single company controls, yet they shape what every firm can charge, borrow and spend. They sit in the 'E' of the macro environment in the PESTLE card.
source_name: US Bureau of Labor Statistics; also Yahoo Finance
teaser_title: America hired more than twice as many people as expected last month, and that could make loans costlier.
teaser: US employers added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment stayed at 4.1%. A strong job market may push the Fed to raise rates. The marketing environment card shows how the economy shapes every business.

headline: Hindalco posts a record quarterly profit of about ₹7,533 crore, up 59%, as revenue jumps 39%
summary: Aditya Birla Group's Hindalco Industries reported consolidated net profit of about ₹7,533 crore for the July-September quarter, up from ₹4,741 crore a year earlier. Revenue from operations rose 39% to ₹91,708 crore and EBITDA grew 42% to ₹13,757 crore. Its India aluminium upstream business lifted EBITDA 55% to ₹7,009 crore, while US-based subsidiary Novelis grew revenue about 25% to $5.94 billion and adjusted EBITDA 20% to $508 million. The copper business also grew revenue by about 47% to ₹21,374 crore.
concept_note: To see where Hindalco's profit came from, you read its income statement line by line and its segment results business by business. How to read those statements is what the financial statements card teaches.
teaser_title: The Aditya Birla metals giant just had its best quarter ever, and it earns most of its money abroad.
teaser: Hindalco's profit rose 59% to about ₹7,533 crore, with Novelis in the US bringing in most of the revenue. Indian aluminium margins also grew. The financial statements card shows how to read where profit really comes from.

headline: Five business groups have proposed over ₹2.4 lakh crore of investment in Bengal since May, led by Adani's ₹1 lakh crore-plus plan
summary: West Bengal has received industrial investment proposals worth more than ₹2.4 lakh crore from five large groups since the new BJP-led government took office in May 2026, Business Today reported. Adani Group has outlined over ₹1 lakh crore through 2035 in ports, logistics, power, roads, green cement and data centres, plus a hospital of over ₹4,000 crore in New Town, Kolkata. Vedanta is weighing ₹70,000-80,000 crore in power and aluminium, possibly near Asansol, JSW about ₹50,000 crore, Shyam Steel ₹15,000 crore at Mejia in Bankura and Jai Balaji ₹6,000 crore. The report notes these are proposals and long-term roadmaps, and turning them into working plants depends on land, clearances and financing.
concept_note: New factories, ports and power plants add to the machines and land a state can use, so it can produce more of everything. That outward push of what an economy can make is what the production possibility frontier card shows.
teaser_title: Adani, Vedanta and JSW have put over ₹2.4 lakh crore of plans on Bengal's table. Will they become jobs?
teaser: Five groups have proposed ports, power plants, steel and a Kolkata hospital since May. But proposals are not factories yet. The PPF card explains how new investment can grow what Bengal produces.

headline: Brent hovers around $100 but heads for a weekly fall of about 12% on hopes for an end to the Iran war
summary: Brent crude rose about 2% to $100.3 a barrel early on Friday and US WTI about 1.5% to $91.8, after Iran said three more tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday. Even so, both benchmarks were on course for weekly losses of about 12%, after an 8% plunge on Wednesday to two-month lows. Traders have been betting that the Democrats' midterm wins will add pressure on President Trump to end the US-Israeli war with Iran, now in its ninth month. ANZ said shipping through the strait was still running below 60% of capacity, and Brent later slipped back under $100 in US trading.
concept_note: Oil prices fall when traders expect more barrels to reach the market soon, even before any extra oil actually flows. Expected changes in supply moving the price is what the law of supply card explains.
teaser_title: Tankers are still being attacked, yet oil is set to fall 12% this week. Hope for peace is outweighing fear.
teaser: Brent touched $100 again on Friday but was still heading for a weekly drop of about 12%. Traders are betting on an end to the Iran war. The law of supply card explains how expected supply moves prices.

headline: Bosch announces a 1:5 stock split and a 3:1 bonus, so one share becomes 20, as quarterly profit rises 19% to ₹840 crore
summary: Bosch Ltd, the Indian arm of the German auto-parts maker, reported quarterly profit of about ₹840 crore, up 18.6% from ₹708 crore, helped by a one-time gain of ₹130 crore, according to Moneycontrol. Revenue from operations rose about 28% to ₹7,655 crore, but the EBITDA margin narrowed to 13.5% from 14% on higher raw material costs. The board approved splitting each ₹10 share into five ₹2 shares and then giving three bonus shares for each share held, which turns one existing share into 20, subject to shareholder approval by postal ballot. Bosch shares fell about 4% to around ₹50,375 in afternoon trade on Friday.
concept_note: A bonus issue moves money from the company's reserves into share capital, but total equity stays the same, so assets still equal liabilities plus equity. That always-balanced identity is the accounting equation card.
teaser_title: One Bosch share worth over ₹50,000 is set to become 20 shares. Does anyone actually get richer?
teaser: Bosch plans a split and a bonus issue together, after profit rose 19%. Owners will hold more shares, but the company is worth the same. The accounting equation card explains why.

headline: India's forex reserves fall $2.69 billion to $717.06 billion, a decline led by foreign currency assets
summary: India's foreign exchange reserves fell by $2.691 billion to $717.056 billion in the week ended October 30, Reserve Bank of India data released on Friday showed. Foreign currency assets, the biggest part, dropped $2.088 billion to $591.118 billion, and gold reserves fell $559 million to $102.591 billion. Reports linked the decline partly to the RBI selling dollars to steady the rupee. Reserves are still about $25.95 billion higher than at the end of March.
concept_note: When the RBI sells dollars from its reserves, it adds to the supply of dollars in the currency market so the rupee does not weaken too far. Using extra supply to hold a price is what the market equilibrium card explains.
teaser_title: India's $717 billion war chest shrank $2.69 billion in a week. Reports point to the RBI guarding the rupee.
teaser: Reserves fell $2.69 billion as foreign currency assets and gold both dipped. Reports link it to the RBI defending the rupee. The market equilibrium card explains how added supply holds a price.

headline: Kolkata jewellers report healthy Dhanteras demand for gold and silver coins, with buyers choosing lighter jewellery
summary: Dhanteras gave Kolkata's jewellers a positive start to the festive season on Friday, with steady demand for gold coins, bullion and silver coins, ANI reported. Vinod Bamalwa of Nemichand Bamalwa and Sons said footfall was slightly higher than last year. He said young working couples now want jewellery they can wear after the wedding too, so light pieces that look heavy are popular. Jewellers said laser soldering lets them make such designs using less gold, and his store is offering discounts on making charges.
concept_note: With gold this expensive, shoppers still buy for the festival but take home less gold in each piece, and coins in place of heavy sets. Buying less of something as its price rises is the law of demand card.
teaser_title: Kolkata still bought gold this Dhanteras, just lighter: pieces that look heavy but use less metal.
teaser: Jewellers saw more shoppers than last year, many buying coins or light, wearable designs. Technology lets them use less gold per piece. The law of demand card explains how buyers adjust when prices rise.

headline: Great Eastern Shipping's quarterly profit more than doubles to ₹1,269 crore, helped by ₹308 crore from selling ships
summary: Great Eastern Shipping, India's largest private shipping company, reported consolidated net profit of ₹1,269.23 crore for the July-September quarter, up 118% from ₹581.41 crore a year earlier. Revenue from operations rose about 47% to ₹1,824.42 crore and EBITDA rose 59% to ₹1,157 crore. About ₹307.90 crore of the profit came from selling ships and other assets, compared with almost nothing a year ago. The board declared a second interim dividend of ₹14.40 a share, yet the stock closed 2% lower at ₹1,430 on the NSE.
concept_note: Money from selling an old ship is a one-off capital receipt, unlike freight income that comes in from regular trading. Separating the two is what the capital vs revenue card teaches, and it explains why investors look past the headline profit.
teaser_title: A shipping company doubled its profit, yet its shares fell. Part of the answer: it sold some of its ships.
teaser: GE Shipping earned ₹1,269 crore, with ₹308 crore from selling ships rather than carrying cargo. Investors were not impressed. The capital vs revenue card explains why one-off gains are treated differently.
